OK, because per the stack trace, AliasedClass forces the mappers to be configured.   no change I make doesn't have some huge caveat I couldn't think of.  the only way to work around this now is to use an event handler for "after_configured" with a global variable; declarative gives you a shortcut using the `__declare_last__` hook:


```python

from sqlalchemy import Column
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey
from sqlalchemy import Integer
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import aliased
from sqlalchemy.orm import configure_mappers
from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship

Base = declarative_base()


aliased_b = None

class A(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'a'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    data = Column(String)
    bs = relationship("B")

    @classmethod
    def __declare_last__(cls):
        global aliased_b
        aliased_b = aliased(B)
        cls.b_non_primary = relationship(aliased_b)

class B(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'b'
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    a_id = Column(ForeignKey("a.id"))
    data = Column(String)


configure_mappers()

print(A.b_non_primary)

```


some other pattern might have to be devised to make this easier.   the non_primary mapper() had the one advantage that it could still make use of the whole deferred configuration system, but building that into `AliasedClass` would be a huge undertaking.  so this is very frustrating.

Well you likely don't need the `AliasedClass` to be global in this case, so it can be simplified:

```python
class A(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'a'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    data = Column(String)
    bs = relationship("B")

    @classmethod
    def __declare_last__(cls):
        aliased_b = aliased(B)
        cls.b_non_primary = relationship(aliased_b)

```

would you be satisfied if I documented the above approach in the [docs](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/13/orm/join_conditions.html#relationship-aliased-class) as the approach to take if mappers are being configured too soon?

So with respect to the relationship I described in my initial post I've converted this:

```py
activity_coupling = mapper(
    TrainActivity,
    join(
        TrainActivity,
        VehicleCoupling,
        TrainActivity.vehicle_number == VehicleCoupling.lead_vehicle_number,
        isouter=True
    ),
    non_primary=True
)

VehicleInfo.current_train_activity = relationship(
    activity_coupling,
    primaryjoin=(
        (VehicleInfo.vehicle_number == activity_coupling.c.vehicle_number)
        | (VehicleInfo.vehicle_number == activity_coupling.c.tail_vehicle_number)
    ),
    foreign_keys=VehicleInfo.vehicle_number,
    order_by=activity_coupling.c.scheduled_start_datetime.desc(),
    viewonly=True
)
```

to this:

```py
@classmethod
def __declare_last__(cls):
    ac_join = join(
        TrainActivity,
        VehicleCoupling,
        TrainActivity.vehicle_number == VehicleCoupling.lead_vehicle_number,
        isouter=True
    )

    ac_alias = aliased(
        TrainActivity,
        ac_join,
        'activity_coupling'
    )

    cls.current_train_activity = relationship(
        ac_alias,
        primaryjoin=(
            (cls.vehicle_number == ac_join.c.train_activity_vehicle_number)
            | (cls.vehicle_number == ac_join.c.vehicle_coupling_tail_vehicle_number)
        ),
        foreign_keys=cls.vehicle_number,
        order_by=ac_join.c.train_activity_scheduled_start_datetime.desc(),
        viewonly=True
    )
```

and it appears to work.  One thing that isn't clear in [this example](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/13/changelog/migration_13.html#relationship-to-aliasedclass-replaces-the-need-for-non-primary-mappers) is that the column names that are referenced in the `primaryjoin` on the `Join` object are an underscore separated concatenation of the table and column names.  It would be nice if you could reference columns on the aliased class directly (but I have no idea what the implications of that would be).

Was also curious if you think passing `flat=True` would have any benefit for this alias; read the docs on that flag a couple of times, but was still having trouble getting my head around it.

With respect to whether I'm satisfied with this approach, it works so that's good enough for me, and I'll  defer you as to whether this is viable permanent solution for implementing relationships of this type.  Thanks again for helping me out with this and the for all the work you do on SQLAlchemy.

btw, workaround with aliased class and relationship inside classmethod works:
```python
    @classmethod
    def __declare_last__(cls):
        j = aliased(ModelB)

        cls.children = relationship(cls,
                                  secondary=j,
                                  primaryjoin=cls.id == j.c.source,
                                  secondaryjoin=cls.id == j.c.dest
                                  foreign_keys=[j.c.dest, j.c.source],
                                  join_depth=0,
                                  viewonly=True,
                                  uselist=True,
                                  )
```
